html:
A species of rice domesticated in West Africa about 3,000 years ago, separate from the far more common Asian rice.

Farmers in the inland delta of the Niger River, in what is now Mali, tamed it from a wild rice that grew in the seasonal floods. It suited local conditions well. Some kinds float up with rising water, others grow on dry uplands, and it copes with poor soils and weeds. It fed delta towns such as Djenné-Djenno.

African rice gives lower yields than Asian rice, and its grains break easily when milled. After the Portuguese brought Asian rice in the 1500s, it was slowly pushed aside, and today it is a small share of West Africa's rice.

Its skills travelled across the Atlantic. Planters in South Carolina and Georgia sought enslaved people from the West African rice coast, and through the Atlantic slave trade their knowledge of tidal rice farming helped build the colonial rice economy. Since the 1990s breeders have crossed African and Asian rice to make hardy new varieties.
sum: A species of rice domesticated in West Africa about 3,000 years ago, separate from the far more common Asian rice.
